Uniform Title: Īśvarasiddhi Main Title: Īśvarasiddhiḥ Secondary Title: Siddhitrayī

Author: Utpaladeva Editor: Śāstrī M. K. Description: Text taken from Volume 34 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies. The *Siddhitrayī* and the *Pratyabhijñā-kārikā-vṛtti* of Rājānaka Utpaladeva. Note: The *Siddhitrayī* consists of three works by Utpaladeva: the *Ājaḍapramātṛsiddhi*, the *Īśvarasiddhi*, and the *Saṃbandhasiddhi*.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 28/11/2005. Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State. Year of publication: 1921.
Place of publication: Śrīnagar | Country of publication: India || Oṃ ||
Now follows the Proof of God (Īśvarasiddhi) composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.
I praise that one God, Maheśvara, who performs all this. || 1 ||
The body, the sense organs, and other such effects are preceded by an intelligent agent, because they possess a specific structural arrangement;
for whatever possesses a specific structural arrangement is constructed by an intelligent agent, like a jar.
Whatever is not preceded by an intelligent agent is not an effect possessing a specific structural arrangement, as [is the case with]...

[The opponent argues: "Atoms, space, a rabbit's horn, and so forth—likewise, the body and other effects possess a specific arrangement; therefore, they must be preceded by an intelligent agent. To this he says:
"The body and so forth have an intelligent cause, because they possess a specific arrangement."
The jar... [is non-existent], like an atom. || 2 ||
Thus [it is said].

And here, by the force of the connection with the subject (*dharmin*), the utility for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which constitutes the probans (*hetu*) is stated. For the jar is established as having clay as its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*); and in that case, there is no possibility of a specific configuration consisting of a broad base and a rounded belly, nor [is such a configuration possible] for worldly activity (*lokayātrā*).

Without a diverse object possessing a specific configuration, there would be a great refutation [of the effect]; and the auxiliary cause would likewise operate only upon that which possesses such a configuration, even when there is a change in color, taste, and so forth—just as the contact with heat in a clear lake [produces changes]. Furthermore, due to the influence of the connection with air, the effect [is produced].

There might occasionally be a change in configuration, but it cannot be a rule; for otherwise, the movement of the wind could occur even without the cause that gives rise to the similarity among the multitude of infinite objects. Or, if [the wind] were the arouser of a single form, then let the wind itself be the intelligent one.
Is it through consciousness... or is it impelled by an intelligent being, just as a jar [is produced] from that? (3)
Thus it is said.

The subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is indeed of the same class as the jar; likewise, [the subject of the thesis] is also restricted to that form, and as the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), it is taken up precisely by way of the predominance of the genus (*jāti*). Thus, the specific arrangement of particular properties constitutes worldly practice (*lokayātrā*).
Furthermore, a sustaining cause that is impossible without a material cause does not exist independently, except through a connection with a cause characterized by independent volition.

By necessity, [birth] occurs through the abandonment of the location of the material cause and the movement to another location. Even the karmas, functioning as auxiliary causes, would produce a diversity of mere form within that state and configuration; however, they cannot produce the characteristic of traversing locations in succession, which requires individual means of accomplishment.
An action that is restricted to the production of a class of homogeneous objects which perform similar causal functions, as designated by their specific arrangement,
must be the effect of that [arrangement]. Even if the action were characterized by the destruction of the conjunction with its substrate,
nevertheless, because the substrate remains in a single state of configuration, such destruction is simply not possible.

As long as its parts have not been moved to another location by an intelligent agent acting with foresight— whether directly or indirectly— this undesirable consequence previously mentioned, [regarding] that which is caused by wind and so forth, remains;
[it would result in] establishing a state of total non-existence.

When one places [the fuel] below, causing it to fall downward, even then another cause—similar to the will [of a person]—must be stated for the fire’s avoidance of its previous location. Even if [the upward movement] were produced by the friction of earthly substances, the refutation regarding the violation of the rule remains as before. Furthermore, when [it occurs] necessarily from the fire...
Through processes such as sweating, cooking, and burning, a substance brings about a different arrangement [of its parts], by which other entities possessing specific genera—
characterized by particular configurations such as swelling and so forth— arise; at that time,
these [entities] possess such forms because they have been produced through the impulsion of an intelligent agent, and not otherwise, according to the reasoning stated previously.

The application of the rule (*niyamayoga*): Thus, this arrangement—which is the cause for the stability of the world, consisting in the movement toward another location, and which is impossible without the existence of material causes—produces, by necessity, the state of belonging to that same class; being in every way untenable in the absence of an intelligent cause, it is observed to be constructed by an intelligent agent.
...devoid of spatial configuration (saṃsthāna). Its object is determined within that very configuration which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā). (4)
Just as in the case of jars and other objects, an intelligent agent is perceived in this diverse [universe]—
a wise creator who possesses the intention for this diverse application [of causes]. (5)
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, this specific arrangement is not unestablished in bodies and the like for the sake of proving pervasion (*vyāpti*). For instance, in the case of a body, the material causes such as semen and blood are established; yet, these do not possess that [specific] arrangement. This is likewise true for the eyes, ears, hands, feet, and so forth.

That very same material cause (*upādāna*) does not possess that [resultant] configuration; likewise, for the worlds—which consist of the arrangement of earthy and other substances—the material causes such as clay and so forth are established as being devoid of that configuration;
there is nothing difficult to establish here. Furthermore, the body and so forth serve as the cause for the protection of worldly life.

This is indeed established for all disputants through direct perception itself; there is no fruit in presenting an elaborate argument on this trivial point. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is indeed established. Thus it is said:
"And there exists causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yoga*) in the case of bodies, worlds, and so forth."
This particular arrangement cannot exist without a material cause.
Thus [it is said].

And this purpose of the proof culminates in the establishment of God (Īśvara). For, as long as there is no knowledge regarding all things—beginning with the body and so forth, which are synonymous with the "universe" and are mutually interdependent—how could there be the desire to create? Thus, omniscience is first established; and likewise...
And because of the capacity for creative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), and because there is no evidence for plurality, the status of being the creator of all belongs to a single [being];
thus, due to the appropriateness of its connection with the specific subject (*dharmiviśeṣa*), it results that the intelligent one is none other than Īśvara. As it has been said:
Thus, here, through the establishment of an intelligent creator, the activity of Īśvara is proven;
for one who possesses knowledge of such diversity could not be powerless. (7)
Thus [it is said].
For in this way, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a particular arrangement is demonstrated with respect to intelligence-in-general alone,
and not with respect to a specific intelligent agent such as a potter or God;
yet that universal form cannot attain stability without a connection to a particular instance— thus, in accordance with the propriety of its relation to the subject (*pakṣa*).

One relies upon a specific individual— such as a potter, a weaver, or some other particular locus— as the basis for one's reliance; just as when fire is inferred from mere smoke at a distance within a grove of *khadira* trees, even though only fire in general is being inferred, the specific quality of being *khadira* [is also apprehended].

Even without depending on a specific instance of smoke, [the probans] is established by virtue of its locus (*āśraya*). For example, when the Sāṃkhya himself, for the sake of establishing the self (*ātman*), puts forward the reason characterized as "being an aggregate" (*saṃghātatva*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) such as the eye, although a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is observed elsewhere— in things like beds and seats— merely by way of their being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), [the self remains] non-composite (*asaṃhata*).

In this way, the supreme Self is obtained through the force of its connection with the subject (*dharmin*); for, apart from the reality of the Self—which is of an uncomposite nature—no other entity beyond the subject (ranging from the eye up to the intellect) is possible. Thus, by the very power of such a thesis (*pakṣa*), that very reality of the Self is [established] therein.

The proof is established; however, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) should not be demonstrated by that very same [instance] regarding the bed, seat, and so forth, for if it were, the example would lack the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), resulting in the fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) due to unestablished concomitance. Nor is the concomitance [to be shown] by way of being for the sake of another in the form of a person who employs [the object].
By which there would be a contradiction because of establishing a purpose that is contrary to one's own position.
Likewise here as well, there is no demonstration of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with either a conscious Lord or a potter.
For this reason, the fallacies such as the unestablished nature of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) are raised. Thus it has been stated by opponents:

"If the supervision of a potter and others is admitted in the case of a jar and so forth, then there would be no supervision by God; if [supervision by God] is admitted, then there is the defect of the example being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*)."
"And as it has been stated: 'If the example were established in that way, the reason would be contradictory' (Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, v. 79).
However, the positive concomitance and so forth are demonstrated merely by means of an intelligent agent, and in the case of bodies and such..."

We establish that the agent is merely of the nature of an intelligent being; however, as this [agent] is established in that capacity, its sovereignty in the form of universal agency comes to be designated by the term "Īśvara" (Lord). In certain cases, such as with a jar, the agent is effectively designated by the term "potter," but not by the status of "Īśvara."
Apart from the intelligent agent inferred from the specific configuration of the universe— including the body, the organs, and so forth—

what else could there be for whose sake one would seek another means of knowledge, since no other causal factor operates here? Indeed, the very activity of all things, such as the body and the organs, which are mutually supportive, constitutes lordship (*īśvaratva*), just as [is the case with a potter].

The very act of being the maker of a specific arrangement of clay is what constitutes "potter-ness. Furthermore, if the property connected to the subject (*pakṣasambandha*) were to be established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), then what would be the distinction between that [specific property] and a mere property (*dharmamātra*)?

Since the latter, due to its lack of restriction regarding place and so forth, is not an object of [direct] valid cognition, this [inference] has as its object only the pervasion (*vyāpti*). It does not [establish the subject-property relation].

[The reason] possesses the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) and is a result [of those characteristics]. Therefore, just as fire, when being established in a certain location by means of smoke in a general sense, is established by implication as being qualified by that specific location which serves as its substratum, and no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required therein; so it is also in the case of proving the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor is it possible to say:

One indeed qualifies fire by means of the exclusion of non-connection with a particular location (*pradeśāyogavyavaccheda*); however, that qualification is established solely through the force of its relation to the subject (*dharmī*), and its establishment does not depend on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). In the same way, here too, an intelligent being would be established as possessing the power to create the universe. Why?
In the case of a specific location delimited by fire, one simply uses the expression "fire";
however,
the intelligent agent of the body and so forth is also designated by the term "Īśvara"— this much alone [is the distinction].
This is the distinction; therefore, there is no room for defects such as contradiction (*viruddhatā*) and so forth. Thus it is said:

"Neither by a potter nor by Īśvara is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) shown here, whereby this [reason] would be contradictory (*viruddha*) or suffer from unestablished concomitance (*asiddhānvayatā*). (8)

Even from the mere demonstration of a pervasion by "possessing intelligence" alone, a particular intelligent being is cognized in a particular instance by the force of the property residing in the subject (pakṣadharma). || 9 ||
Just as, when the state of being a composite is observed merely on the basis of subservience to another [an alternative reading is *īkṣate*].
Because of its suitability in the case of the eye and other [senses], the Self is held to be non-composite and supreme.

Or, just as from smoke seen at a distance there is the establishment of fire in a grove of *khadira* trees, that [fire] is established as being specifically *khadira* by the very cognition of it. (11)
Thus [it is said].
Nor is it the case that a specific arrangement characterized by the unique particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a jar or the like is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
thus, that very [arrangement], when observed elsewhere in a subject (*dharmin*) for which an agent has not been seen, establishes only an agent of the same class as those previously observed.
But it should not be said that [the object] is merely a name for a configuration, because it is not established that such a universal form (sāmānyarūpa) is an effect;

for [the object] is indeed the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Although an effect is cognized through perception and non-perception in relation to a particular characteristic, nevertheless, that particular characteristic is established as an effect in that very way.

It establishes even other individual particulars (svalakṣaṇa) of the same class as being effects of other individual particulars of the same class that serve as their causes; just as a single instance of smoke, once established as an effect of fire, establishes that all other instances of smoke are likewise effects of fire. And that—

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an effect is homogeneous with other various particular characteristics by virtue of being produced by multiple cooperative causes (*sahakārin*). Thus, for example, the particular characteristic of a jar is homogeneous with anthills and the like through its being made of clay,
with cloth and the like through its configuration, and with [other round objects] through its sphericity.

By means of such sequences as earthenware bowls made of flour and so forth, or felled trees and the like— being distinct from one another— the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) possessed of their respective classes are established as having each their own specific cause and effect.
Even by the Buddhists, this systematic arrangement is maintained for the purpose of employing a cause of a certain class when there is a desire for an object of that same class.

This is stated by those who say that the configuration belongs to the clay and not to the potter, and that the nature of being clay does not derive from the potter. If this is indeed the state of affairs, it is because a cloth is not produced by a specific intelligent person in the same way that a jar possesses its configuration; and the cognition regarding both cases is exactly the same.

Furthermore, activity proceeds for the sake of the realization that [an object] is created by an intelligent agent; such is the very determination [of our position]. Just as those other Buddhists must necessarily admit that "homogeneity" exists even without a universal (*jāti*), and that the capacity to produce a single cognition is based solely upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), so too [is it for us].
This too [is established]:
since a particular arrangement and so forth are observed to follow the presence or absence of a certain kind of controller, that [controller] is inferred from it.
Otherwise, from the cause of some transformation of clay belonging to a potter,
such as a jar and so forth, the production of an anthill would also be established as his work.

Such statements of theirs are devoid of any consideration for their own previously stated arguments that effect a distinction [between universals and particulars]. For the utility of separate causes applies only to universals, qualities, actions, or other properties, precisely because they reside in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Because the accomplishment [of the purpose] is faultless, the arrangement itself— when qualified by its suitability for mutual causal efficiency (arthakriyā) and so forth, as in the case of women, men, and the like— is indeed non-deviant as a proof for the agency of God regarding the body and other such things. Thus he says:
And thus, in this case, the cause is specified merely by its configuration;
it is characterized by its mere variety, not by the definition of a specific individual essence (*svalakṣaṇa*). (12)
Even by those others, when distinguishing the self from the jar through various reasons, the wise maintain that the status of being a cause belongs solely to the configuration (saṃsthāna). 13.
This entire universe, distinguished by specific configurations capable of mutual causal efficiency, is rightly fashioned by the Lord.
Thus [it is said].
10) Here the Sāṃkhyas object:
This might indeed be so if each individual thing were the cause of something else; however, it is [in fact] only a plurality [that acts as a cause].
Through a continuous association with undifferentiated place, time, and other factors, each [cause] attains the status of being the specific condition for the manifestation of that particular effect.

Consequently, those factors which, having entered into a state of coexistence, bring about the appearance of the effect, are seen to exhibit diverse modes of activity in their mutual conjunction. For instance, water, earth, and so forth, become seeds by entering into the interior of the seed.
Due to the transformation of the sap and other elements, they act as cooperative causes for the sprout, which possesses a long and accumulated configuration.

Even activity, characterized by the reaching of another location, is not perceived as anything distinct from the form itself, such as a transformation occurring in that very place. Therefore, just as there is a transformation at every moment in the same location of the single material cause, so too [is it here].

If it were to exist by way of being situated in another location, what contradiction would there be? This fault applies to the acceptance of the immutability and permanence of entities, but not to the doctrine of momentary transformation; for just as in the case of entities such as wind and fire, their movement toward other directions occurs without restriction, so too is it in the case of [other] entities.

Due to the association with such specific auxiliary causes, they would necessarily be capable of producing an effect of a similar nature that is fit for its purpose; even if this were so, nothing would be faulty. Furthermore, an entity established through the connection with a perceived object does not serve as a basis for the postulation of an unperceived one.

Even if one were to postulate a Lord (Īśvara), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. All proponents of philosophical systems must admit the diversity of the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of things, by virtue of which a sprout arises from a seed alone and a jar from clay alone; therefore, [the effect arises] solely from a particularity induced by the superior capacity of auxiliary causes (sahakārin).

Entities that arise by moving to another location, possessing a configuration distinct from their material cause (*upādāna*), do not admit of verbal designation [as being identical to that cause]. However, in cases where auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are employed in producing effects while remaining situated externally in their own locations—
such as a lump of clay, a potter’s wheel, and so forth— there is a dissimilarity between the arrangement of the material cause and the resulting effect.

There might be an opportunity for one who possesses intelligence, just as in the case of a potter; for if the mere material cause possessed parts capable of moving to another location, it would have been so even previously.

Furthermore, in this case, the mere employment of an intelligent agent does not everywhere establish such a fixed rule for auxiliary factors that sustains its status as authoritative. As it has been said:
"In this regard, it is replied: the course of auxiliary factors is seen to be manifold."
Some might somehow or other come to encounter [them] through their appropriations.
Others, possessing causes, having entered and attained the nature of the material cause (upādāna),
indeed fashion their effects, just as the juices of the earth and water do.
Others, moreover, revolve externally within the appropriation;
they are not so capable as to produce the variety of forms in effects. (17)
In that case, even if the scope of what is called "the intelligent" is postulated, a systematic order would not be established everywhere by that alone. (18)
Thus [it is said].

(12) Thus, having established the variety of modes of operation among causes as they function toward a single effect in the form of that effect, [the author proceeds to describe] the characteristics of all the constituent parts, such as the body and the instruments, which are under discussion—

The primary cause, designated as *pradhāna*, which effects all things, has already been established without contradiction through the presentation of arguments such as "homogeneity" (*samanvaya*) for the proof of *pradhāna*; thus, it is not a subject of inquiry here. For the refutation of God (*īśvara*) does not occur merely by the establishment of *pradhāna* as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
Because the *pradhāna* is established as the fundamental cause precisely at the level of the atom;

and if that *pradhāna* were merely to refute the atomic theory (*paramāṇuvāda*), then the system of *pradhāna* would become an object of knowledge (*prameya*) in the context of an inquiry into the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the universe, but not otherwise.

In the process of establishing the efficient cause: thus, the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), consisting of the equilibrium of the three qualities known as sattva, rajas, and tamas, is by its very nature as *prakṛti* characterized by productivity;
through the qualities themselves entering into the relationship of primary and secondary factors, it [evolves] into the form of transformations beginning with the Great One (mahat).

As long as it undergoes transformation, the very fact that it serves the purpose of the *puruṣa* is its inherent cause therein. For it is not by mere chance that the entire range of effects— consisting of divine, human, and animal births,
possessing their various intermediate species, and invariably characterized by the two forms of female and male— is produced.

Mutual compatibility is established; this very thing, in the form of a specific arrangement, is also accepted by the proponent of God (Īśvaravādin). This [compatibility] belongs to all these transformations, together with their primordial material causes (prakṛti), which exist in the state of both manifestation (vyūha) and pervasion (vibhava).
The mutual relationship of parts and whole, resulting from a specific arrangement for the sake of worldly subsistence, would thus be purposeless; as it has been said:
"In that case, this rule for the arrangement of actions would not exist."
"Accidental...

and so forth. Furthermore, the meaningfulness of everything that has the nature of an object culminates, through a succession of stages, solely in the accomplishment of the perception of pleasure and pain; for even objects that are present and come into the vicinity [of the senses]...
They are conceptualized as being like the horns of a hare;

therefore, through the longing for consciousness, by virtue of being its object, they possess the very nature of being enjoyed— thus, [the distinction] from the enjoyer even in relation to the enjoyed.

Since the reality of the Self, whose very nature is consciousness, is already established, the employment of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed untenable. Although phenomena appearing on the plane of the mind also indicate that the reality of consciousness is manifest even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nevertheless...
That [intellect], being manifested as turbid by the coloring of the object, existing as an object of experience, impure,

and characterized by non-distinction from the state of being an enjoyer— precisely because of this, the reality of the Self, which is purely the witness consisting solely of consciousness, is inferred.

This occurs by virtue of the relationship between the possessor and the possessed—which is synonymous with the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed—and not because it directly becomes an effect. As it has been said:
"O, by what means could one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
Thus, it is by the mere proximity of that [Puruṣa] that the manifestation of the forms of objects which ascend into the mind occurs;

otherwise, it would be impossible for an insentient entity to become such through its own power. Therefore, although in reality the activity of the transformation of Prakṛti is not for the sake of the Puruṣa, it is described as being for his sake because its purpose is to produce a variegated manifestation dependent upon him.

If the transformation of the qualities were for the sake of one another, then one among them would successively possess the nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), because the function of consciousness (*cid-upayoga*) is fully realized in every transformation. And it is not possible for a single entity to possess a nature that is both conscious and unconscious (*cid-acid-rūpa*), consisting of absolutely distinct classes of being. That very point...

At one time it is inert when it is the benefactor, because for the non-inert conscious self (*cidātman*), there can be no transformation into the act of benefiting another; and at other times it is non-inert when it is the beneficiary. However, unity is not possible when such a contradiction exists, nor indeed can there be the state of being a beneficiary for that whose nature is pure consciousness alone.

It proceeds as follows: by coming into contact with the assistance provided by the objects that have become its limbs (subsidiary parts), there arises the contingency of an excess over its conscious nature, which results in the attainment of insentience. For this very excess is indeed what constitutes insentience.
Thus, as long as it exists in the relationship of limb and possessor of limbs, or beneficiary and benefactor, it remains subject to insentience.

It is indeed the object-field that is the enjoyer; however, there is a metaphorical designation of the person as the enjoyer because, in its proximity, the mind—possessing the form of the object—manifests itself.

And thus, by the admission of these qualities (guṇas), there follows the consequence of their attaining the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatā), which results in the loss of their status as qualities. For this very reason, it is not logical for them to have their own objects; for that single [consciousness] would then incur the state of being both the contradictory enjoyer and the enjoyed. Therefore, all of this is unstable by nature.

The function of the *guṇas* has as its sole purpose the consciousness of objects residing within the mind, witnessed by the unfluctuating *cittattva*. Whatever variety of objects is capable of being perceived, all that perception is designated as the "purpose of the *puruṣa*" (*puruṣārtha*), serving as the cause for the activity of the transformation of the *guṇas*; and such is the object of perception.

The qualities (guṇas) exist in states such as the extremely subtle, and likewise there is the distinction between the qualities and the Puruṣa. Therefore, just as the perception of the Puruṣa’s purpose— which consists of the experience of that which is other [than itself], namely pleasure, pain, and delusion— is the goal of the Puruṣa,
so too is the apprehension of the distinction between the qualities and the Puruṣa through the means of knowledge taught in the treatise, such as inference and analogy.
Both of these are the purpose (*prayojana*) because they consist in the activity of the qualities (*guṇa*) toward enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

Furthermore, the nature of being capable of accomplishing that purpose is called the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). However, a future purpose that has not yet occurred cannot function as an efficient cause. And in that regard:

When the purpose of the Self, which culminates in discriminative knowledge, has been fully accomplished, the *guṇas* no longer function for the sake of that Self due to the absence of a cause for their activity;

thus, isolation (*kaivalya*) is said to belong to the Person, even though he is eternally isolated. This being the case, [the agency] of the clay, the staff, and so forth, is [merely] inherent to them...

Let there be an intelligent potter as a cooperative cause for the production of individual objects such as jars, and likewise a weaver for threads and so forth; however, by that much alone, no one distinct from well-known causes need be postulated at the time of the production of the body and other such things. This is so that there may be no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the argument.

Moreover, the differentiation of form and so forth in effects such as jars and sprouts is indeed established through the specific capacity of perceived causes like the [material] substratum; likewise, the manifestation of specific configurations would also arise from that very capacity—what fault is there? Why then posit an unseen factor (adṛṣṭa)? For in whatever form...

Or rather, the human purpose attains its establishment through a particular configuration; in that regard, the cause is simply the very nature of the *guṇas*, because it is established in that very way. And it is precisely through the favor of that nature that the body, objects, sense organs, and so forth [come into being].

Even merit and other such actions may serve as efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for a collection of effects that abide in states preceding and following the mind; beyond this, one who imagines further [causality] would surely be disregarded as having strayed from the path of reason. This much alone constitutes the eightfold [power].

Mastery over the mind, like [mastery] over the dharmas and so forth, is sometimes manifested; that which co-exists with the guṇas alone brings about the designation "yogin. However, that which is superior to this—eternal, belonging to a particular puruṣa—is [the mastery] involved in the fashioning of bodies, instruments, and worlds, as well as in creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

It would attain the status of a cause only by disregarding the existence of its own primordial nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*), which is non-different from it and serves as the basis for the manifold variety of purposes conceived for the sake of the *puruṣa*, and instead by relying upon something separate that is established through mere devotion alone.
Regarding this, he says:

Furthermore, according to the principle already stated, no further distinction can be established for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

For, since it would otherwise entail insentience and a lack of sovereignty, how could this Lord— who, like merit (*dharma*) and other qualities, occupies a level within the field of the mind— possess a manifest state of consciousness within the primal cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) in order to undergo the transformation into effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*)?

An instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa) might be postulated here. In that case, if it is the previous transformation— which produces successive modifications appropriate to the purpose of the Puruṣa— that is the instrumental cause, then let that very nature of the purpose of the Puruṣa be the instrumental cause even for the entire mass of transformations up to their final specific particulars.

What is the use of adhering to the logic of the "half-old woman" (the partial application of a rule)? Thus it is said: "In that case, [the state] of this [puruṣa], which moves within the internal organ, resides in the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti). (24)
Thus, the state of being the cause of transformation would be attributed to Īśvara.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) does not depend on any other efficient cause for its transformation into the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, because it has as its sole nature the transformation into the modifications of the elements for the sake of the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*). Whatever has as its sole nature the transformation [into something else]...

In that transformation, it occurs in such a way from its very own nature (*svabhāva*) without depending on any other cause, just as the collection of causes such as the seed does in the transformation into a sprout. And that which does not occur in such a way without depending on others does not possess such a nature in that regard, just as a rice seed [does not produce a barley sprout], or as a seed lacking water and so forth [does not produce a sprout].
And thus, the Pradhāna has as its sole nature the transformation into evolutes such as Mahat and the rest, which are useful for the purpose of the Puruṣa;

it is not like a rice seed [producing] a barley sprout. Therefore, the Pradhāna undergoes transformations such as Mahat and the rest solely by its own nature, without depending on external instrumental causes such as Īśvara and so forth. Herein, the Pradhāna...

This [conclusion] is indeed established by means of reasons such as "concomitance" (*samanvaya*) and so forth. Furthermore, its nature as the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*) has been demonstrated by the negation of its being for one's own sake (*svārtha*) and other such attributes.
As for the example—the collection of causes such as seeds—it does not possess the status of being the "subject" (*pakṣa*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubted by the opponent.

And since that [seed] has precisely the nature of producing that sprout, its independence—its having a nature that does not depend on anything else—in producing its own effect in that manner toward that [sprout] is not at all doubtful. Thus he says:
"Whatever has transformation as its sole nature, in that case, it [arises] from that [cause]. (25)
Just as the causal complex of seeds and so forth is independent of anything else with respect to the sprout,
[so too is the primordial matter] whose nature consists in the transformation into the flood of evolutes such as the Great One (mahat). (26)
And the *pradhāna* consists of the three *guṇas*; therefore, the Sāṃkhya is without a Lord (*anīśvara*).
Thus [it is said].

For if it is argued that in the production of all variously configured effects, the very fact that the *pradhāna* exists for the sake of the experience of the *puruṣa* is itself the efficient cause, and what need is there for a Lord (*īśvara*)?

In that case, what would the potter contribute toward the making of the jar? Even there, the clay lump and other materials belonging to primordial matter (pradhāna) would possess the capacity to produce a jar endowed with such a configuration solely by virtue of being subject to the nature of the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha). For [the jar] cannot exist without the configuration of a broad base and a bulbous belly.

Would the enjoyment obtainable through the fetching of water by the enjoyer be accomplished [by that action], or would it be by the actions of those seeking grass, water, and so forth? Would the jar possess that particular form [only] because of the potter being there? Or is this too merely a specific nature of the *pradhāna*, such that in the arrangement of the jar and so on...
Just as there is dependence on an intelligent agent in the case of a staff and a wheel, so too, by that same collection of primal causes (*pradhāna*),

the production of an object such as a jar— which possesses a specific arrangement for the sake of human purpose— is accomplished. In the very same way, how could the body, the sense organs, and other such effects not arise from the primal cause (*pradhāna*) given its inherent nature?
The dependence upon an intelligent being capable of acting accordingly is not required; for this is the established principle:

when the relationship between smoke and fire has been understood once in one place, at another time and in another location, the same relationship between those very same types of smoke and fire must necessarily exist, such that even unobserved smoke [indicates the presence of fire].

Fire is inferred [from smoke]. By this very same logic, since a connection with an intelligent agent is perceived in one particular arrangement, it follows that the same applies to every such arrangement everywhere.

Since the invariable concomitance with an intelligent agent is established even by the structural arrangement of the body and so forth, why is there no inference of such an intelligent being from the unseen (adṛṣṭa)? Thus it is said:
"If [the unseen] possesses the nature of serving the purpose of a person in all purposeful actions... (27)
Primordial Matter (pradhāna) is postulated as the efficient cause;
for without that potter, how indeed could even a jar come into being? (28)
[The opponent argues: "From the very lump of clay consisting of primordial matter (pradhāna), [the jar arises] due to its suchlike nature;
or else, this dependence upon the potter and so forth is simply its inherent nature. (29)
"Likewise, they depend upon Īśvara by their very nature for the sake of the body."

Nor can a diverse arrangement, useful for human purposes, be produced merely by the entry of auxiliary causes into the material cause, even if there is no operation on the part of anyone who intends a specific utility. For instance, as long as this [effect] arises from this [cause], it cannot again arise from something else that possesses only a slightly greater degree of excellence.

Thus, by this specific distinction, this very thing becomes possessed of a particularity; furthermore, from this very same [cause] when endowed with another particularity, an entirely different effect—one of a different genus—is produced. Therefore, at present...

If one does not possess an intellect skilled in reflection such that it considers, "This is what is required; I shall act accordingly," then how could there be the acts of rejection and acquisition for the sake of performing such specific actions? Furthermore, even if one were wise, the constant occurrence of such effects would not happen for that intelligent person at all times.

Because there is an absence of the desire to produce that [effect], even that [desire] must be required by it; for if the essence of water, earth, and so forth— devoid of the pursuit of desire— were to enter into the material cause (upādāna),
the result would merely be something gross and undifferentiated, rather than one characterized by specific utility and division.
The modes of arrangement of their parts are seen to be diverse in all these cases;

yet they are not absolutely distinct from one another, for as long as they are capable of performing a single purposeful action, they are perceived as belonging to the same class, depending on the conjunction and disjunction of various auxiliary factors brought about by an intelligent agent.
If the capacity belongs solely to the auxiliary factors devoid of intelligence (*buddhi*), it is appropriate that the mere effect takes the form of doubt;
for a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*) of the division of parts would exist in one case, while in another it would be of a different nature entirely.
Furthermore, that which possesses concomitance (*anugāmitva*) necessarily follows the specific mode of its application.

It is observed in all effects; otherwise, such [regularity] would not exist by necessity. Therefore, the activity of an intelligent being’s will and so forth is seen to bring about the various arrangements and divisions—such as jars, bowls, water-drawing pots, and bricks—derived from a lump of clay, in accordance with specific purposes.

It consists of a specific excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*), and not as a cooperative cause by virtue of being a mere receptacle for something heterogeneous to insentience. For if that were the case, then due to its connection with the potter, it would produce only a jar or only a shallow bowl, but not a basin, nor even bricks and so forth. Therefore, he desires and knows how to produce [the effect] exactly as it is.

In this case as well, there is the emergence of a specific effect. For this very reason, the particularity of the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) is sought after because of its utility for the purpose of a person (*puruṣārtha*), and not merely because of its shape—such as having a broad base and a bulbous belly—which might lead to the objection: "It is established that such-and-such is the nature of the presiding agent," and so forth. [This occurs] together with desire (*icchā*).
For even the arrangement [of parts] would lack finality if it were further dependent upon hands and so forth; therefore,
there must be a single being who knows the mutual compatibility of the body, the instruments, and the world.

Likewise, the agent possesses a specific capacity for arranging [materials] solely according to his will. Although a carpenter may possess knowledge of the arrangement of iron in the case of a plowshare and the like, nevertheless,
due to his lack of practice in manual operations such as those involving the hands, the blacksmith alone is the agent in the forging of iron.

However, for one who possesses the synthesis [of knowledge] regarding things existing in different places and times, as well as their transformations and so forth, when an effect is accomplished by mere volition alone, the dependence on another agent is not established in respect to any portion of the universe;
just as a blacksmith does not depend on manual practice [for each individual act], there is thus only one creator of the universe, such as bodies and the like.

This is because it is useful for human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, this state of being sought after by a multitude of seekers does not depend on a mere jar; rather, since it is found in jars, cloths, carts, and so forth, and because it is produced by an intelligent and capable agent, the subject inferred is one of such a kind, and not merely someone who has seen a jar-maker, just as [in the following example].

In the inference of fire in general, which proceeds from the means of valid cognition consisting of perception and non-perception regarding various fires such as those made of grass, leaves, or wood, and their respective smokes— since the causal relationship is established based on the universal (sāmānya) when multiple particulars are observed, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the particular.

It is established; and because the deviation from one particular instance entails the certainty of deviation from all particulars, there is no need for the observation of all particulars, since this does not exclude particulars such as the *śaṅkha* and *pāṭī* which have never been seen before. Thus, here too, it is only a matter of a particular configuration.
Furthermore, since one observes various configurations resulting from the desire to produce such things, once the general relationship of cause and effect is established,
and once it is ascertained that specific agents such as a potter or Īśvara are excluded due to deviation, [the existence of] a body that has never been seen before—

By not excluding specific intentions to act, such as those involving instruments and so forth, there is an inference of mere intention from the specific configuration [of the effect]; for, even though non-omnipotence is not a constituent factor in the effects of desire,
one accepts its requirement based on mere co-observation.
Any effect produced by will—such as instruction and so forth—would be established whether [the agent] were the Lord or not the Lord;
furthermore, since we observe that will coexists with attachment to a body and other such factors, those possessed of will would not produce such effects in the case of silver mines and the like.
Thus, the diversity of the structural arrangements of bodies, instruments, and worlds [is explained].
Without the greatness of wisdom corresponding to that [reality],
how could there be a discernment of utility arising from the mere nature of insentient matter produced by primordial matter (*pradhāna*)?
It would follow that [the self] is necessarily persistent and the locus of desire; therefore he says:
"Not at all, because of the entry of the material cause into the midst of the auxiliary conditions. (30)
Even a specific arrangement [of atoms] can be produced;
this is possible only through wisdom that attends to the course of worldly affairs, for nothing else suffices. (31)
Likewise, without the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), the emergence of a diverse arrangement would be mere grossness alone, and not useful for the world. (32)
If it is argued that a creation, though diverse in form, must necessarily follow a fixed order because a jar is produced merely through the cooperation of a potter; 33.
The body and so forth would never exist, nor would there be even a long lump of clay;
therefore, because it is that which is sought after, the specific arrangement [of parts] is distinguished.
That [atom], which fulfills one's desire, is not established as being a jar or the like;
nor is it here under discussion as being either a Lord or a non-Lord, for its characteristic is that of an atom. (35)
"He who produces variety wherever it occurs is accepted as the Lord (Īśvara) therein."

Furthermore, since there is no manifestation of *pradhāna*— the very root cause— through volition and the like, how could it possess a connection with desire and so forth brought about by the aim of the *puruṣārtha*, from which activity would arise?
And although the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses the functions of desire and synthetic reflection, nevertheless...

As long as this [light], though manifesting, has not become an object of cognition due to the proximity of a person, it does not assume the form of will and so forth; for such is the defining characteristic of the synthesis of will and the rest. Otherwise, it would be something entirely different. And that being the case, [it would not be will].

The activity of the intellect (*buddhi*) alone constitutes the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); even the person's own cognitive operation would be a purpose for the person, but it is not the case that the primary cause (*pradhāna*) alone or cognition alone is the purpose of the person. Therefore, [the activity of] the primary cause, the intellect, and so forth, exists independently of the person.

It is indeed correct that "being for the sake of the person" (puruṣārthatā) should not be predicated [of the intellect], because such a thing lacks the nature of being a pursuit of purpose; thus, it is logical. Now, although the single principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), known as the Great One (*mahat*), which is common to all persons, truly possesses a function characterized by ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) that differs for each individual, [it is still not the person].

Or rather, let this function—determination and so forth—belong to the instrument known as the mind (*manas*), which is born from the Great Cause (*mahat*) or from the I-principle (*asmitā*). Let it be restricted to each individual *puruṣa*. It is not tenable that by means of that [function], occurring at a later time, the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) or the Great Principle (*mahat*) possesses a desire to pursue the purpose of the *puruṣa*; rather, [it belongs to the mind].
At the very moment the Pradhāna undergoes its first transformation, there arises a desire for universal coordination directed toward all Puruṣas.

The first function, such as determination (*vyavasāya*) and so forth, is indeed designated as "intellect" (*buddhi*), by which it would follow that even this [primal nature] acts preceded by intellect. That too is not tenable, because the primary [nature], being entirely unmanifest in form, has a function that cannot be perceived. Nor [is it tenable] regarding the function...
If [the activity] were unknown to the Puruṣa, it could not take the form of intentional pursuit and so forth;

yet, by whom could the activity of Pradhāna be perceived even by the Puruṣa? For its activity is universal, directed toward all Puruṣas. If it were perceived by each individual Puruṣa, then that Puruṣa would possess omniscience, and [Pradhāna’s] purpose would consist solely in the fulfillment of that individual's aim.
As before, it is useful to all persons because it possesses the capacity for attending to its own effects;
and although the state of being the locus of manifestation— which is a property of that which is to be manifested—
is infinite due to the proximity of infinite persons, it is nonetheless [considered one] by virtue of the unity of its substratum.

Because they mutually uproot one another, the plurality of Puruṣas is not established. Now, if it is argued that the state of being perceived belongs to a specific Puruṣa who is omniscient and exists in a universal form, such that he perceives the activity of the universal Pradhāna—then let him alone be Īśvara;
for his very desire to create the universe, being perceived, becomes the connecting link, just as in the case of Pradhāna.
For that [Pradhāna] as well, it is because of its connection with being a causal condition (nimittakāraṇa), and because of its omniscience and its being the creator of all. Thus he said:
"And there is no possibility of desire and so forth in the Pradhāna, nor the state of being for the sake of the Person. (36)
For since this [cognition] of his, though it might arise, would be impossible without being experienced by the person;
such being the case, there is the fulfillment of the human purpose.
Even for the person (*puruṣa*), that [cognition] would not belong to the *pradhāna* alone;
nevertheless, the function of the mind (*manas*) or the intellect (*buddhi*) is refined by each one individually. (38)
How could desire be useful for all human goals?
Rather, it belongs to Pradhāna, which is common to all. (39)
That [desire] of a person would also be unperceivable; for whom could that desire be perceivable?
If it were perceivable by everyone, then omniscience would follow for every single individual. (40)
If [the objects] were distinct yet appearing as such, they would become confounded due to the unity of their illumination;
or else, [they would be so] by means of some single entity that is non-different from all persons. (41)
"That which is to be known is indeed this one; he is the agent, the knower, and he is the Lord."

Now, if human purpose (*puruṣārthatva*) belonged only to that which possesses the intention, "I shall act for the benefit of the *puruṣa*," then it would not belong to the *pradhāna*, because such an intention is absent in it; rather, whether it be the *pradhāna*,
the *mahat*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), or even semen and blood, they possess it precisely because of their inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
It brings about such an effect that, once it has arisen with its various configurations and so forth,
a cognizer seeking a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) perceives it from afar and joins it with another, just as one joins a man and a woman.
Furthermore, in some cases, due to the force of karma, there may occur a fortuitous or otherwise accidental convergence of obstacles and other factors;

consequently, one might metaphorically say that the causal factors operate for the sake of the *puruṣa* (the Self), as if for the purpose of his enjoyment, and thus attribute "purposefulness for the *puruṣa*" to them. However, even this is not tenable, because if this were the case, in reality...

Since there is no efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), it is by their own nature and independently that causes produce such specific effects; yet, when the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* has been perceived, why does that very same activity toward producing effects not also occur for that [liberated] *puruṣa*? Or rather, does it indeed occur for one [liberated *puruṣa*] through *prakṛti* alone?
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that [bondage] ceases for a single person simply through the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*?

Since all *prakṛtis* are of a uniform nature, how could there be a capacity to serve as a means for all *puruṣas*? Let that be so regarding the eight *prakṛtis*; however, as for semen, blood, and the like, they relate to the *puruṣa* who is considered liberated.

Why should it not produce an effect consisting of a body? Or rather, even that does indeed occur for it; however, because the Puruṣa has already achieved its purpose (*kṛtārthatva*), that which has arisen does not reach the state of being fully experienced by him. This would be so only if the Puruṣa were to exert some effort characterized by a modification of its own nature (*svarūpātiśaya*) for the sake of experiencing the intellect (*buddhi*).

It might be argued that [the Spirit's connection with the intellect] has now ceased because its purpose has been accomplished; however, since the Spirit is at all times devoid of intention, devoid of effort, uniform, and indifferent, there can be no occasional conjunction with excellence for it, nor any subsequent cessation thereof, as that would entail the loss of its immutable nature (*kūṭasthatā*). Due to the power of karma, a specific modification (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) of the intellect—or rather, of the internal organ—is determined for each individual person; by means of this, the liberated person experiences the cognition of another’s mental modification. Otherwise, there would be no cessation of the experience of the mental modifications belonging to one's own self alone; therefore, [this is] for the sake of the person (*puruṣa*).

Since there is no distinction between having desires and being free from them for that which is by nature eternally liberated, the internal organ— being restricted by the karma of the self— would be experienced solely through karmas during the state of bondage.

At the stage of liberation (*mokṣa*), however, it does not arise at all; otherwise, because the state of the *karmas* would remain unchanged, how could there not be a necessarily determined experience for the specific person concerned? For *karman* is not the regulator of persons.

Now, for one whose karma is exhausted, the internal organ... [does not exist].
The nature of being an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatā*) is what is being discussed; what, then, is the proof for this?

Furthermore, at that time, bondage and liberation would have to be accepted as resulting from the presence or absence of karma, and not from conjunction and disjunction; consequently, there would be a contradiction with [your own] doctrine. Moreover, actions do not [arise] even through compassion.
Acts such as giving would cease for one who has realized the nature of the person; furthermore, if it were accepted that actions motivated by passion and hatred possess the quality of bondage,
one would simply be resorting to a philosophical view that asserts bondage and liberation are caused by the presence or absence of passion and so forth.

In the doctrine of an inherently existent person (*svābhāvikapuruṣavāda*), even for one who has discerned the distinction from the person, liberation would be impossible because the cessation of the connection with the intellect (*buddhi*) would be untenable;
thus, by the impelling of another conscious person, that [activity] belongs to the root cause.

The activity directed toward producing specific arrangements useful for cyclic existence is thus logically established; therefore, the presentation of the previous reason is entirely faultless. As it has been said:
"One would not produce a seed that generates a sprout out of a mere intention for worldly subsistence. (42)
However, by its very nature, that causal complex of his is such that a wise person would join together those things that have arisen as mutually compatible. (43)

If it is argued that its status as a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) is stated by way of that metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then even when that human goal has been accomplished, [the scripture] would still be directed toward that person. (44)
Does the primal cause not cease its transformation into its own effects,
or does it never cease within this supreme group of seven natures?
For that single [entity] is indeed perceived by all persons through its transformation;
nevertheless, the transformation of the body and so forth occurs by its very nature. (46)
Why would it not be as before in the case of that one who is considered liberated? Or, even if it does indeed exist, why is it not joined with him? (47)
Because he has achieved his purpose through the liberated soul, he is devoid of desire and remains solitary;
for there never exists such a lack of desire in this person or in his mind.
(29) "Because the desire [for the body] has ceased, there would be no further union with a person.
This too is not logical, since the consciousness residing in the body has already arisen.

If, because its nature consists solely in being an object of experience, that [liberation] does not occur through the destruction of karma, then liberation would necessarily have the destruction of karma as its basis, consisting precisely in the very nature of that [destruction]. (50)
Even for those who have realized the distinction between the self and the non-self, their actions may arise from compassion and other such motives; they do not arise from passion.
If this is so, then liberation must result from the destruction of passion. (51)
And thus, the abandonment of perception would follow; therefore, the perception of intrinsic nature is not tenable.
Consequently, it is established that the body and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent. (52)
This proof, "because of the difference in configuration," is faultless. (53)
Thus [it is said].
This very reason, when applied toward the Supreme Lord, [functions] by means of its own inherent nature.
Nor is he ever overcome by defects in reasoning, whether slightly or even by another; this alone is what is being stated. || 54 ||
Even though established by thousands of brilliantly shining logical arguments, [the truth] does not reach realization for those of deluded minds;
even though Maheśvara is present in the palm of one's hand, [he is not perceived].
The true jewel flees from one who is struck down by fate. || 55 ||
This very Self alone, the Lord within all living beings,
flashes forth as both the agent and the knower, provided that it is supreme.
Recognition is what is to be proven;
and that has been established by us elsewhere, but here it is for the sake of proving the Lord (Īśa).
Even in the case of duality, it is fitting that [the truth] exists; at night, the fire shines all the more intensely.
Thus ends the *Īśvarasiddhi*, composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Utpaladeva, son of Udayākara.
By the command of the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra, this [work] has been prepared and published by Madhusūdana Kaul for the delight of the virtuous.
